summary: Extends IKEv2 so peers can periodically repeat mutual authentication, which matters in remote-access setups. This limits how long a third party who has taken control of a peer can keep using security associations. It is experimental.

eli5.summary: A guard asks you to show your ID again every so often, so a thief who grabbed your badge cannot use it for long.

subtitle: Requires periodic re-authentication to limit unauthorized access duration

tldr.problem: In remote-access VPNs, if a third party gains control of a client, they can continue using stolen security associations until they expire, potentially weeks later.
tldr.mechanism: The responder sends an AUTH_LIFETIME notification specifying when the initiator must repeat the IKEv2 authentication exchange, forcing fresh credentials.
tldr.outcome: Organizations can limit how long a stolen VPN connection remains valid, forcing periodic user re-authentication.

today: RFC 4478 is an Experimental extension to IKEv2. It remains in use for remote-access VPNs where periodic re-authentication is required by security policy.

sections.title: The Re-authentication Problem
sections.content: IKEv2 (Internet Key Exchange version 2) establishes encrypted tunnels for remote-access VPNs. In many remote-access scenarios, users authenticate once and then use the VPN for hours or days without re-authenticating. If a third party compromises the client and steals the security association, they retain access until the SA expires. This document extends IKEv2 to allow periodic re-authentication, requiring the original initiator to repeat the authentication exchange at intervals set by the responder.
sections.eli5: When you connect to a VPN, you prove who you are once. But if someone steals your connection, they can keep using it. This makes the server ask you to prove who you are again after a set time.

sections.title: The AUTH_LIFETIME Notification
sections.content: The responder (VPN server) sends an AUTH_LIFETIME notification to the initiator (VPN client) specifying the number of seconds before re-authentication is required. The responder can send this notification in the final message of the IKE_AUTH exchange or later in an INFORMATIONAL exchange. The initiator SHOULD repeat the Initial exchange within the specified time. If the initiator fails to re-authenticate, the responder may delete all security associations. The lifetime field is typically set to reasonable values: at least 300 seconds (5 minutes) to avoid burdening users, and no more than 86400 seconds (1 day) to maintain security benefit. A zero value means re-authentication should begin immediately.
sections.eli5: The server tells the client "come back in 2 hours and prove you are you again". If you do not, the server closes the connection.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility
sections.content: Older IKEv2 implementations that do not support AUTH_LIFETIME will simply ignore the notification and not re-authenticate. In such cases, the responder can manually close the connection by sending a DELETE notification. The mechanism does not require both sides to support re-authentication; initiators can enforce stricter re-authentication policies than the responder requests, and the notification does not override initiator security policy.
sections.eli5: If an old client does not understand re-authentication, the server can just drop the connection. Newer clients can ask for re-authentication more often if they want.
